utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you and you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And also good morning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I represent Mr. Naser Oric. Together with us are our legal assistant Ms. Adisa Mehic and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we call in -- before we bring in the witness? Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, just one, Your Honour. Following the meeting yesterday on Rule 98 bis we said we would revert to you regarding what sort of a time estimate we were considering, and we have considered the position very carefully in light of the discussions with Your Honours about the new oral procedure and precisely how that should unfold, and in light of that we consider that actually we would opt for a more summary presentation of the arguments rather than taking Your Honours through a detailed exegesis of the evidence which has been given which of course is unnecessary because you're well aware of the evidence. So in light of that, we would opt for, as I say, a more expedited presentation of between an hour and a half and two hours, and of course, with the possibility of elaborating on any points or any evidence which Your Honours would wish me to but we could certainly do it that way, enabling, if Your Honours wish, the whole proceedings to be concluded that week. So just to give you that indication. And I informed my learned friend on the Prosecution bench this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Jones. And also I thank you even more for having thoroughly grasped the reasons, the purposes, behind the amendments that we introduced to the rules and for being very cooperative with the Tribunal, with the Trial Chamber. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Taking this as a start of the proceeding and also the Prosecution abide by the expeditious way to deal with oral pleadings, we will be ready to start the submissions by the 3rd of June, meaning on the Friday and to use that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So I thank you also, Mr. Wubben. You have been most cooperative throughout as well, understanding the whole purpose behind these amendments, which moves very much as I tried to explain earlier the burden that it's thrown on the Defence in particular in a party-driven motion or system as regards the motion for acquittal on to the Trial Chamber, which has now got the onus of protecting the rights of the accused in this area, the right not to be compelled to answer charges that we believe he shouldn't be made to answer, and that thrusts a tremendous onus on us to make sure that we reach the correct decision. So I thank you both and we will hand down a scheduling order accordingly in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, the witness, please. You would be able to finish today, Madam Vidovic, won't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I don't think I will need more than two hours, maybe even less. It will all depend on how the witness answers my questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I ask you because I imagined that would be your answer basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. I hope you've had time to rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will proceed today with your testimony, and Madam Vidovic, who is lead counsel for Naser Oric in this trial, will cross-examine you. After that, we'll see whether there is any re-examination, any questions from the bench and soon after, you can go home. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could I please ask you to remain -- for me to remain seated during the cross-examination? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brkic.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order for this part of the proceedings to be as expedited as possible, I'm going to ask you a number of yes-no questions, and if you can only answer with a yes or a no, could you please do that and this will certainly save us some time.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you have a lot of military experience and knowledge, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You worked as an infantry officer and then you occupied high positions in the military judiciary system of the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For six years I was in infantry and the rest of the time I was in the legal services.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, you drafted a number of military regulations of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you supervised their drafting, you didn't author them, you prepared and compiled a number of documents that you spoke of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, isn't it, that in all that, you used your academic knowledge, your memory and that you did not refer to the JNA manuals because at that time you did not have them at your disposal; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even when you were in Sarajevo, during the terrible shellings at the beginning of the war, it was not easy to come by professional military literature and regulations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When withdrawing from the barracks and facilities that they had, the former JNA took their documents with them, and this included regulations, laws, manuals and other things; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume that this is correct but I can't be sure of that. I don't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the Ministry of Defence in Sarajevo, some of the Serbian staff that had worked in this ministry took the manuals and professional literature with them. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since that kind of literature was missing from the premises, it is to be assumed that the literature had been taken away, at least this is what I can assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, you did not find any such literature on the premises; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony and especially when you gave your statement to the OTP, which you did, don't you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You explained that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not adopt a single law or regulation of the JNA verbatim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In a certain way, the only exception was the decree law on the adoption of the service in the armed forces and its application in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a republican law. This law was passed on the 11th of April, 1992, and it was published in the Official Gazette of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, issue number 1?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask Madam Usher to show the witness P286.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the decree law that I have just mentioned that was passed on the 11th of April, 1992. Could you please take a look at this decree law, and based on this decree law I'm going to ask you some questions. It is correct, isn't it, that this decree law on the adoption of the law on serving in the armed forces and its application as republican law of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina contained only a small percentage of the provisions that originated from the former regulation of the JNA. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was less than 10 per cent of the original law.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness another document. This is Exhibit P543. For the record, this is a decree law on the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was published in the Official Gazette, issue number 4/92, in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, could you please take a look at Article 42 of this decree law? First I'm going to quote the end of this provision or this article. On the day when this decree law starts being applied, this will supersede -- I'm quoting paragraph 2 of this article -- "this will supersede the decree law on the takeover of the law of service in the armed forces and its application in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a republican law." Mr. Brkic, I'm right in thinking that this document was in force only for 49 days and it was made null and void by the decree law on the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was published in this Official Gazette, issue number 4/92, in May 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 49 days and this decree law was made null and void. It was superseded by another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was exactly the purpose of my question and thank you very much. On your testimony yesterday, you were shown Article 2 of this decree law. Could you please take a look at it again?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well then.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me quote part of it: "Armed forces of the republic are composed of the army. In case of a war, the armed forces, in addition to the army, will also be composed of the police and the such armed forces which will be placed under the sole command of the armed forces of the republic." With this regard, Mr. Brkic, I'm going to ask you to explain something. It is correct, isn't it, that there were proposals for the police to be placed under the command of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina never issued a decision to such an effect. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were several attempts for the units of the Ministry of the Interior to be placed under the sole command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, for certain personal reasons, or personnel reasons, rather, this never took off the ground, save for one case when the reserve forces of the Ministry of the Interior were placed under the sole command but only pro forma in order to accomplish a certain combat task, and there is a decision of the Presidency to support that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just for better understanding, when you say the units of the Ministry of the Interior, you are actually referring to the police. This is what we refer to as the regular police?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the regular police units, there were also units of the special police. So that the units of the Ministry of the Interior consist of several specialties, so the uniformed police, the police that patrols the street, are not the only units of the Ministry of the Interior. There are also special units which perform special tasks. This decree law does not specify any units but I suppose that the implication was to place under the sole command all the units of the civilian Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this explanation. Therefore, for certain combat activities, the police had to be resubordinated to units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina by certain special orders. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only way. There had to be a special order or a decision by the Presidency as the army Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Otherwise, the police had its own civilian command, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, during your testimony, you said that the military police, according to our regulations, was within the composition of the armed forces in terms of its organisation, and I have something to ask you about this. It's true, isn't it, that the internal structure, the strength, and in which commands or units of the army the military police units would be was something that was determined by organisation and formation?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the organisation formation of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained yesterday the way in which the rules governing the service in the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were drafted. Can the usher now please remove this previous document, and I would like to show the witness a new document. This is Prosecution Exhibit P544. Just for the sake of the transcript, these are the rules governing service in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Witness, can you please have a look at the date --

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I don't think this is the right document. You're talking about the rules governing service; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One at a time, please. Could the speakers kindly speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please go to the relevant page? I think that must be the last page, or rather the last portion of this document, and please look at the date.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Thank you very much. So you agree this was passed on the 1st of August, or at least that's what the date appears to indicate. In relation to that, let me ask you something. These rules were adopted before the decree law on the ratification of international conventions regarding international law of war and -- which was passed on the 23rd of August, 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I see in the protocol number and all the other evidence that would seem to be correct. But I did explain yesterday that for a time all the regulations of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were drafted in parallel. Only the day of the actual passing or adoption differed. There depended on when a meeting of the Presidency took place. But in relation to what you just asked, the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance yet again please. I would like to leave there copy of the rules with the witness. We may be requiring it a little longer. And can you please also show the Witness OTP Exhibit P271, P271. This is the decree law on the ratification of international conventions regarding the law of war and other related judicial matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please have a look to see what this document is about? In your testimony yesterday my understanding was you said you had not personally drafted this document but you had supervised its drafting or in some way supervised the drafting of this document you had been involved, had you not?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Through a colleague of mine, a subordinate who was working with the Ministry of Justice at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at this list, you will agree, won't you, that the list contains, or rather, if you look at this decree law, you will agree that it contains a list of ratified international conventions regarding the international law of war?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Can you just please have a look? I'll leave the document with you for a minute or two, although I'm sure you're familiar with the list in its entirety. But do you agree with me that The Hague Convention, number 4 from 1907, which relates to the customs and laws of war on the ground is not on this list? Can you please have a look?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to go back to the document and have a look briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that I've been able to see, I don't notice that it is on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, can you perhaps help us with an answer, why is it that this convention that relates to the laws and customs of war did not come to be included in the body of international law that was adopted by Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you could give us a hand with that, please?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion, as I explained yesterday, that it was because of the absence of precisely these provisions at that very difficult time that most of the international conventions, or rather bilateral treaties from this convention didn't make it into this provision. We simply had no insight. We didn't have these documents available, and we could not submit this to the Presidency for ratification for purely technical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To this very day, in fact, Bosnia and Herzegovina has not ratified this particular convention. Is this something you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please? I would like to show the witness -- we can have this document removed, and I would like to show the witness a different document now. The document I'm talking about is OTP Exhibit P319. So for the sake of the transcript, this is a decision of the Presidency on the application of the rules of international law of war in the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 23rd of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony yesterday, the Prosecutor showed you this order. Can you please now go back to Articles 2 and 3 of this order on the application of the provisions of international law of war? I will quote paragraph 1 of Article 2 and paragraph 1 of Article 3. Paragraph 1 of Article 2 says: "The commanders of the units shall be responsible for the application of the international law of war and each member of the armed forces individually." And then paragraph 1 of Article 3 says: "In order to learn the rules of the international military law, the armed forces shall organise training regularly which shall be obligatory for all members of the armed forces." During your testimony yesterday, you confirmed this order placed the responsibility on the shoulder of the commanders of the units, as far as the application of these rules was concerned?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that -- or rather, do you agree with me that these commanders should either have the necessary knowledge regarding the international law of war or should have a copy of these rules available to know what they are about and what their obligations would be?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order to inform their own soldiers about these rules and organise training, they would likewise need the required knowledge or the alternatively the documents that we have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I need to add something. As the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia had been adopted, which governed the same area in a manner of speaking, as educated and well-trained people they would have been expected to be familiar with this. But in answer to your question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that as generally well-educated people they would be expected to be familiar with this area, you mean the commanders who would have been expected to have a decent level of education?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander should certainly be expected to have a decent degree of both military and civilian education which would make it possible for them to exercise their duties as commanders in a proper way. Military commanders who complete military schools during their time at these military schools also study these regulations and do acquire a decent degree of general background.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brkic. Throughout the war, you were in touch with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina one way or another throughout the war, I say, and you were familiar with the situation in its ranks. Do you agree with me that throughout 1992 and 1993, there were the great number of commanders in the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who had not received any military training or any training at all, generally we could say that there were a great deal of commanders with little or no education at all. Do you agree with me when I say that?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say over 90 per cent of them were like that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I had tried to restrain myself as much as I could but my attention has been drawn as we go along. You both speak the same language and because of that, you're not allowing that very short interval of time between question and answer and between answer and question to allow the interpreters sufficient space and time to be able to interpret completely to us. Please, try to cooperate as much as I -- as you can. I know that this is not easy. Sometimes we do the same thing when the rest of us speak English, and I appeal to you to try and do your best to allow that short interval of time. Thank you. And not to speak too fast also because you both are speaking very, very, very, very fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I see that your last answer was reflected in the transcript, so now I wish to go back to the international conventions that we discussed. In your testimony yesterday you explained that even when you were in Sarajevo there were no copies available to base the new provisions on. Rather, you had to go to Zagreb to get copies in order to work with these.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was something that the Ministry of Justice did, and I'm not sure how they came by these conventions, but I know there is a Zagreb edition that was obtained, and it took about 20 days to track these documents down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, even you, who were in Sarajevo, had no copies available of these international conventions to work with them. You simply did not have any copies available, did you?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they might have been available somewhere but the defence ministry or the justice ministry simply had no copies available based on which they would have been able to draft these provisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to go back to the rules governing service in the armed forces. I think you still have a copy in front of you, don't you? I think the witness still has a copy there.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just look through it briefly?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to look through the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. You're familiar with these rules, and there is a question, a very general question, that I'd like to ask you in relation to this. It's true, isn't it, that this law of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is to a high degree different from the former law from the former JNA. This law contains 81 articles and the same document of the JNA had over -- contained over 600 provisions. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about the provisions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina governing military discipline, you said that when you were drafting these documents, you were using the JNA laws as a mere blueprint. It was just something you used in order to make sure that the new provisions would encompass all the aspects of this subject matter. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You, therefore, were involved with drafting most of the new provisions and regulations governing the work of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's true, isn't it, that the regulations of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were drafted to serve the purposes of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was a country with a totally system from the one that prevailed in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the military regulations of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were created in an entirely different time frame and in the midst of a war, with war conditions prevailing, which was a very different situation from the situation in which the JNA provisions were created?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were no military regulations. These were regulations of the civilian authorities which pertained to the army or rather the armed forces. These were passed by a legislative body. These were civilian regulations governing the work of the armed forces. At that time, and given the kind of system that was in place at the time, and given the realities of the international situation, these were laws that were the result of the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, also they were inaugurated as such and applied as such by the various bodies and organisations in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for this explanation of terms. Let me ask you this: It would be wrong to say, wouldn't it, that the customary practice in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was to use different rules and regulations of the former JNA. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question well. However, I can say that with a certainty that the regulations of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that applied in the life and work in the army were not used in the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were absolutely not applied unless for maybe the 49 days while the first set of rules was in force. This is the decree law on the adoption of the law governing the service in the army in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was superseded in -- after 49 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you commented upon some provisions of the decree law on defence.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, not the decree law on defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you looked at the decree law on defence; it's Article 42, if I'm not mistaken. However, I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness P286.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This will be of some assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the same document we saw earlier on in the beginning of your cross-examination this morning, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is something that I spoke of yesterday. On its first page this document has two decree laws. The first one is on service in the armed forces, and the other one is on defence. I'm interested in the second decree law, the decree law on defence. The exhibit -- the exhibit number, however, is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in any case, I believe that you saw this document yesterday, and I would kindly ask you now to look at another aspect of this law. Could you please look at Articles 35, 36, 37 and 38. After you have found them, I'm going to put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that I would like to say that I did not provide any comments on this decree law yesterday. I didn't work on this decree law. I only attended the session of the ministry when this decree law was adopted by the government. However, I had not participated in its drafting.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But you were present?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can provide some comments, but I didn't work on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You were present when this decree law was adopted and you are familiar with the contents thereof. Could you please look at Article 35 of this decree law and the other articles that I've mentioned? I'm going to read to you Article 35. On its territory in the frame of its rights and duties determined by constitution and law in the system of defence of the republic, municipality organises defence and protection, civil protection, monitoring and reporting service, communication and cryptographic data protection, and it also conducts other preparations for defence in case of war it organises all people's resistance." Can you then please look at Article 336? It says here: "In organising and implementing of defence, the municipality will carry out organisational material and other measures for the realisation of citizens's rights and duties and defence." After that, items 10 and 11 in this Article 36 states that the municipality will organise preparation for defence and defence training. That it will take care of preparing of territory for defence needs. And now can you please look at Article 37 just briefly. This article says that the municipality is duty-bound to ensure the enforcement of regulations and other enactments of the Republic Presidency, the assembly, the government and ministries. And then can you please look at Article 38, which reads: "In the realisation of rights and responsibilities in the field of defence, the municipal assembly determines on issues of importance for defence," amongst other things. Let me ask you the following: This decree law was in effect for at least as up to July 1993, and these provisions were never changed, not before the end of the war. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with these provisions, I'm going to ask you the following questions. It is true, isn't it, that after the passing of the decree law on defence in May 1992, municipalities were the bodies that were duty-bound to organise the conditions, organise everything that was necessary in order to prepare for defence?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with this decree law and decree law on districts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to the district -- to the decree law on districts a bit later. Thank you very much. Military commanders, pursuant to the law on defence were not the ones to create preconditions for the functioning of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. They were not duty-bound to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, you mentioned the fact that during the war the republic was divided into ten counties or districts, and a while ago you mentioned -- a little while ago you mentioned this decree law on districts. It is true, isn't it, that the decree law on the establishment and work of districts, which was published on the 13th of August and that I'm going to show to you in a minute, courtesy of the usher, regulated the same matters. Now I would kindly ask the usher to show you this decree law. I'm referring to an excerpt from the decree law on the establishment and work of districts which was published on the 13th of August, 1992 in the Official Gazette, number 12/92. Witness, could you please look at page with ERN number 01194713, and can you please look at Article 3 of the decree law on the establishment and work of districts. Article 3, I'm going to quote it to you: "The district shall ensure that the basic material and other means of the armed forces and population are met, as well as the efficient and uninterrupted functioning of the political system." And now let me put a question to you. It is true, isn't it, that the districts and the municipalities by law were duty-bound to provide material and other requirements that were necessary for defence, and that by regulations they were the ones that were duty-bound to provide for the functioning of the state organs on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This is a general provision, Article 3. And Article 8 is the article that elaborates on those obligations in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please turn to a different page and look at Article 8. The ERN number is 01194714, Article 8, that is, and this article refers to the rights and obligations of districts. Could you please look at item 6 of Article 8? It reads -- it is very brief. It reads: "Through its bodies, within the scope of its rights and duties, the districts will organise armed combat on the territory of the district and leading this combat." In other words, districts and municipalities, pursuant to the regulations that were in effect in 1992 and in 1993, I'm talking about the period between 1992 and 1993, districts and municipalities were duty-bound to organise armed combat in their respective territories, to lead this combat and to create preconditions for such combat. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, because at the time there were still a Territorial Defence and there was no army as a special system.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The districts had their defence secretariats that were in charge of organising defence and combat. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the districts were duty-bound to create a prerequisites for the army that would enable the army to function according to rules and regulations?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Judging by this decree law and the decree law on defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, that it would be absolutely wrong to consider that this was something that commanders were duty-bound to do?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Commanders were not duty-bound to do anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These provisions were in effect for at least up to mid-1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't have all the amendments that were introduced at different times, and I cannot confirm the exact date when the first amendment was introduced. So I cannot be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have an exhibit number for this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, since you have told us that you don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, I apologise. This document already has an exhibit number, or maybe not. I don't have any information about this document having an exhibit number at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what's the next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document which is being tendered by the Defence is being marked as Defence Exhibit D282.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you well? Did you say that you had those amendments before you? Could you please look at the first amendment that was introduced in 1993, if you have it before you, and could you tell us whether there were any amendments to the provisions that we have just discussed?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any amendments in 1993. I have three in 1992. The first one on the 13th of August, 1992, the second one on the 7th of October, 1992, and the third one was on the 9th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me if I say that these provisions that I quoted to you were never amended by any of these amendments?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. They were never amended.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask the usher to show the witness another document. This is the decree law on amending the decree law on the establishment and work of districts. It was issued on the 18th of August 1992. I believe that you already have the document before you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 13th of August. I emphasise that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. 13th of August, thank you. I'm going to quote to you from this decree law on amendments to the decree law on the formation and operation of districts. I'm going to quote Article 1: "The decree law on the formation and operation of districts after Article 60 shall be changed and it shall read as follows: In municipalities in which the president of the municipality was not elected pursuant to Article 273 of the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall appoint the Presidency of the municipality who shall serve in office until there are conditions for the election of the president by the legal organs of the municipality." And with this regard let me put the following question to you. This question is very important in this case. This amendment to the decree law established the procedure to organise the so-called War Presidencies of municipalities. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume this because I don't know what the author's intention was when he drafted the law and its amendments. I was not familiar with this area. However, in congruence with the constitution, and you have it here in the collection, the appointment of commissions and War Presidencies, this was published in the Official Gazette and I believe that this is what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Article 273 of the constitution regulated the duties and rights of the municipalities, didn't it? I can quote it to you.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well then. I'm going to show it to you very soon. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for this decree law on amending the decree law to be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And this will become Defence Exhibit D283. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if I can have the usher's assistance, please, I would like to show the witness the following document. It's a document that we have. This is the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the appointment of the members of the War Presidency of the Municipal Assembly of Srebrenica dated the 2nd of September, 1992. Witness, I would like to draw your attention as well as the attention of the Chamber that the defence has included Article 273 of the constitution that applied at the time, so please, if you could first go back to Article 273 of the constitution that applied, it's the one I asked you about a while ago, as soon as you receive it, of course. Article 273 is, I believe, on the last page of this set of pages.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that I was not involved in the drafting of this decision. I'm not familiar with it. I can also say that the signature is authentic. The signature indeed belongs to the president of the Presidency. As for the substance --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, but I'm about to ask you a different question with regard to this. We mentioned Article 273 of the constitution a moment ago. Its substance was included in -- or rather attached to this decision. It's on page 3. You have a total of 3 pages. If you could please look at Article 273 of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In relation to this, I would like to quote a portion of the decision and ask you a general question, not something about the very -- the functioning. You may be able to help us or you may not be able to help us but here you go. I'll ask you the question anyway. I'm quoting paragraph 2. Paragraph 1 appoints the member of the War Presidency, Murat Efendic, and I'm drawing your attention to Article 2 which says: "The Presidency of the Municipal Assembly of Srebrenica will work as decided by Article 273 of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina for so long as conditions are created to elect the members of the Presidency by the legal authorities of the municipality of Srebrenica. The Presidency shall exercise its functions as soon as possible in the free part of the municipal territory and make sure that all the other state bodies and organisations are functioning properly." Witness, I have a general question to ask with regard to this. War Presidencies, to the extent that you were aware, or in as far as you can confirm, had the responsibility to decide on issues within the jurisdiction of municipalities, including any situations in wartime circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was pursuant to the decree law on the formation of districts and Article 273 of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It was the War Presidencies also that had the responsibility to ensure the conditions were in place for the work of other state bodies, organisations and institutions across the municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Much like the Presidency on behalf of the republican assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the same applied to these other people on the ground, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The district presidencies, as far as subordination was concerned, the Presidency -- on behalf of the assembly, the Presidency, and the Presidency of the district on behalf of the district, and the War Presidency of the municipality on behalf of the municipality as the governing body of the municipality, until such time as conditions were created to go back to every day normal work.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document please be assigned Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, Ms. Vidovic. I see that it is composed or it consists in three documents. The first one is precisely the decision of the president of -- of President Izetbegovic appointing or electing the members of the War Presidency of the Srebrenica. Then there is an extract from the Official Gazette of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina dating back to February the 25th of 1974, and it relates to a decision on proclaiming the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And finally, there is an extract from the constitution of 1974, being Article 273. Do you plan to present them all together as one document or separately?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. But may I just clarify this? We have an established practice when we tender exhibits to put on the first page of each document so that we know which document we are dealing with, and I want these two documents to have just one exhibit number, not two separate numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I never meant to tell you or to suggest to you that they need to be two or three different numbers. I just, for the record, said what the document itself or the exhibit consists of. And this is going to be marked as Defence Exhibit D284.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, it's true, isn't it, that the decision to establish district military courts, according to the regulations that apply where we come from, could only have been adopted by the highest organ, the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should have been a law on district military courts which could only have been passed by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina acting on behalf of the assembly and no one else.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The court itself could not have been established by any of the local authorities and military commands, rather, they could only have been established by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by their own decision?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there were exceptions that were envisaged by law.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The commander of the municipal staff of the TO under the rules was not responsible for setting up a military disciplinary court; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military disciplinary court? There were the rules issued by the defence ministry saying that units between the level of squad and brigade should have first-instance courts and a higher court with the staff of the military forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can show the witness another document, please. If the witness can please be shown the document bearing the ERN number 01858075.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document produced by the defence ministry based in Sarajevo. The date is the 19th of January, 1993. The document was signed by the deputy Defence Minister, Mr. Munib Bisic. Can you please have a look, Witness? I want you to look at paragraph 1 of this document. It reads: "The rules and military discipline regulate the organisation of military disciplinary courts, using a two-stage system." Second paragraph reads: "First instance military disciplinary courts shall be founded at district headquarters, attached to district defence staffs on the order of the commander of the district defence staff." And then we go on to the third paragraph, I quote: "The high military disciplinary court was formed by order of the Minister of Defence dated the 3rd of October, 1992." And paragraph 4, if you could please look at the last part, it says: Those who commit disciplinary violations shall be brought, or rather the corps commander was the only officer who had the authority and the responsibility to adopt a decision to have someone who committed a crime tried by a military disciplinary court. Up there you have Article 52 which says that those who committed a criminal offence should be placed before a court by the commander of the district defence staff. Do you agree with me that after the corps were established during this period of time the corps commander, and I'm talking about 1992 and the beginning of 1993, the corps commander was the only officer who had the authority and the duty to bring all those who committed crimes before a military disciplinary court?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's obvious that there is a certain amount of confusion in this document. On the 18th of August -- I was not aware of this up to now, by the way. The 18th of August 1992, as the date of the establishment of the BH army, the -- Article 41 of the law governing the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina was transformed, and on that very day the work of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina ceased to apply, and what started being applied at that time was the provisions as they were drafted in relation to the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In relation to what you just asked, what that means is that from that day on, district staffs and municipal staffs of the TO lose their authority, the authority that they had, pursuant to certain regulations. And as far as criminal prosecution was concerned, this was something that was taken over by the commands, or rather the corps commanders as this order clearly states.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was in fact applied throughout 1992 and part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're referring to. What was applied?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What you just confirmed, that the corps commanders took over the role --

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the 18th of August, 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, before we move on to the next question. I noticed that on this document, in the left-hand top corner, third part, that refers to the 3rd Corps command in Zenica. Would the same situation described in the rest of the document obtain also to the 2nd Corps command, or was this something that is applicable only to the 3rd Corps command? I'm putting the question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, yes. This applied to all units of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd, the 4th, and the 5th Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, all alike.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification, Your Honour. Can this document please be assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will become Defence Exhibit D285.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, sir, I'm about to ask you a different question now. For some reasons that I'm about to present you with, it was in the very nature of your job, if I ask the question from the viewpoint of this Defence team of course, in the first half of 1993, you were rather well informed on the situation that prevailed in Srebrenica. You were a member of a working group that was working on the agreement for demilitarisation. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we need to rephrase this. I went to the airport three times, together with a team of military officers, in order to conduct negotiations with the Serbian side, under the aegis of UNPROFOR. And the person in charge was the English general named Hayes. I attended these meetings three times, in a bid to establish a protected zone. But that was the extent of my involvement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Be that as it may, you are familiar with these negotiations surrounding the demilitarisation agreement, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that I've just described and no more.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did see the agreement itself, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't there for the final meeting when the agreement was reached and signed. I wasn't there. If I remember correctly, there were about five such meetings and I only attended three.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Brkic. I will still ask you to please have a look. It's Defence Exhibit D276, and this is the demilitarisation agreement. I will be asking you a couple of general questions about this document, nothing very specific. When considering the demilitarisation agreement, can you please have a look. This is a document signed by General Sefer Halilovic and by General Ratko Mladic. What I wish to draw your attention is item 4, the last two sentences, please, of item 4. In order to save time, I will quote what the agreement says: "No armed persons or units except UNPROFOR will remain within the city once the demilitarisation process is complete. Responsibility for the demilitarisation process remains with UNPROFOR." I'd like to ask you a question about this. You attended those meetings, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that requests were being made and eventually granted that each and every armed soldier should leave the territory of Srebrenica after the 18th of April, 1993. This is something you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is something that was said at the meetings that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This applied to the military police and the military security organ in as far as there was any such thing, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police, the military security, well, we are talking about the armed forces. That's all they are, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this applied to them equally, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's only logical. They were part of the armed forces, so the same thing applied to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for this. I won't be asking you any further questions on the demilitarisation agreement since you appear to not be familiar with the agreement itself or its implementation. Let me ask you a different question. You testified that you had drafted regulations and that there were certain rules according to which these regulations were eventually published. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, you do not know, do you, whether the regulations that you testified about yesterday were eventually forwarded and delivered to all the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know, and it wasn't part of my remit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at a document, the document I'm talking about is Prosecution Exhibit P162. OTP Exhibit P162. For the record, this is information that the Presidency of Srebrenica municipality sent to the Tuzla district Presidency. It was signed by the president of the municipality of Srebrenica, Hajrudin Abdic, and its secretary, Esed Nukic, on the 25th of May, 1993. Mr. Brkic, could you please take a look at the page with ERN number 01840618. I'm going to quote to you -- you know what the situation was in Srebrenica in the past, we did not receive any Official Gazettes, we did not receive any regulations, so the decree laws that you're referring to are not known to us. The Official Gazettes, number 1 and 2/93, that were sent to us were the first sets of regulations that we received from the beginning of the war. Can you please turn to the next page of this document. On page 3, which is paragraph 4 in the English translation, it says: "We also kindly ask you to send us all the necessary sets of regulations and particularly the regulations that were adopted in the course of 1992 and 1993." With this regard, Mr. Brkic, let me ask you this: Judging by this information, the most important sets of regulations that you had worked on and those that were passed throughout 1992 and even some that were passed in 1993, because the document mentions two acts, never reached Srebrenica or so it seems.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this information they are talking about the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, issue number 1, which mentioned the appointment of the Territorial Defence command; and number 2, which carried the adoption of the laws of the former Republic of Yugoslavia as the republican laws. These are the two sets of regulations that they are referring to. They are not referring to the Official Gazettes of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a compilation of the regulations published in the Official Gazette of the state Official Gazette. And if you will allow me a comment, it can be concluded based on this, I can not claim with certainty, that they did not have any Official Gazettes but the two and they wanted all the Official Gazettes to be delivered to them, but this was delivered by the publishing house, not the army or the government. There was special delivery envisaged but the situation was what it was and what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you agree with me that in 1992 the most important decree laws were passed and published, those that were relative to the application of the international humanitarian law and those that were relative to the service in the BiH army, the military discipline, the district military courts, the district military prosecutor's office and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Up to the 23rd August 1992, we passed all the regulations that regulated the normal life and work in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. With this regard, let me ask you this: You cannot provide us with a confirmation that any of these sets of regulations that you testified about and that you have just mentioned ever reach Srebrenica during that period of time. You never heard that this had been done?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only to Srebrenica but to any unit of the BiH army. The only compilation that I had was this one that I have before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that I printed, that I was authorised to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to have a very short group of questions, and maybe this is a good moment to take our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness a document immediately. This is P544, and this is the regulations governing service in the BiH army signed by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 1st of August, 1992 and published in the Official Gazette of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, issue number 2/92.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I would like to draw your attention to Article 29 of the regulations. Yesterday the Prosecutor showed you some other provisions but I would like to turn to another aspect of these regulations.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about the accommodation of units?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to quote one part of Article 29, which refers to the accommodation and keeping order in the units. And I quote: "The units and institutions of armed forces may be billeted in the barracks in a camp, in a military airport, on a naval ship, and in other military facilities of that sort. As the units are deployed, the most importance has to be paid to providing for combat readiness and security of units and institutions and the formation groups must not be broken." With this regard, I would like to ask you the following: The rule envisaged, didn't it, that units should be billeted in barracks, camps and military facilities; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in military institutions, but in barracks, camps, military airports and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is how it was provided for combat readiness of units as well as for the control of behaviour of the troops. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, that if this rule could not have been honoured and the units were not billeted in barracks or camps because there were no such things, and if troops stayed at home, the possibility to control the troops was either minimum or non-existent? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask at this point that that is a question more of speculation, certainly not related to the regulations that he has in front of him. Now we are asking for his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let us draw the conclusion, Ms. Vidovic. I don't think it's fair on the witness to put that question to him. Yes, objection sustained, in other words. Or you can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order to control the troops, they would have to be accommodated in barracks, camps, in keeping with this rule?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When adopting these provisions, you confirmed to the fact that members of the BiH army, in order to enjoy the protection under the rules of war, had to be provided with appropriate uniforms. Before that, Mr. Brkic, let me ask you this, in order to clarify things. Yesterday you told us that it was indispensable to pass laws and create a legal framework within which the units of the BiH army could participate in an armed conflict and put up forces against the aggression that came from both Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Is it true, then, that it was necessary to pass certain laws and regulations and to create a legal framework in which the units of the BiH army could operate and participate in an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When these provisions were being passed, you accepted the fact that members of the BiH army, in order to enjoy the protection under the rules of war, had to be provided with appropriate uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the standards of the Geneva Conventions, those parties which are party to the war did not have to have uniform to be considered members in the war. Not all the members of the army had uniforms. They had some markings and some insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: They had to have recognisable insignia showing that they belonged to the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And conditions were prescribed for uniforms, markings, ranks, insignia and other things that show that the person was attached to the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Without these insignia, the lily as the symbols of the army, they could not have been recognised by the enemy as members of the BiH army; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, at the beginning of the armed conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, members of the then Territorial Defence had IDs measuring two by two centimetres in size with the coat of arm of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is a shield with a line and three or six lilies on the coat of arms, and they would put that marking on the most prominent part of their uniform, not uniform but clothes, either on their chest or their arm or their cap, and this was a symbol that they belonged to a certain state, the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and its Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And without those insignia, they could not be identified as members of the army by the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be logical, but I said that the Geneva Conventions standards prescribe what elements a certain party had to -- has to comply with in order to be considered a party to the conflict. What you're asking me is something that I can confirm, somebody cannot be recognised without an insignia, and it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that is the reason why you passed, amongst other things, the rules of recognition and the insignia on uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The logistics service of the Territorial Defence or the armed forces drafted a special regulation on uniforms and insignia and other external markings of members of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fighters who did not wear the BiH army uniforms, who did not openly carry weapons and who did not have recognisable insignia would not necessarily enjoy protection under the rules of war if they became prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a legal question which I cannot and won't answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I thank you. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there will just be a brief re-examination, and I would ask if the Court would just allow me three minutes, I need to check some information that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we need to stay in the courtroom or do you --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you mind if we take a five- or ten-minute break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, this is what I am suggesting because we will be -- in view of everyone in the meantime. I suggest we take a five-minute break, and we will resume and finish and conclude soon after all right? We will be staying outside the courtroom. As soon as you're ready, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. --- Break taken at 11.12 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. My re-examination will be fairly concise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I would ask that you be shown Prosecution Exhibit 271 again. We have discussed it. It's the ratification of certain treaties.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You were asked on cross-examination as to whether the 1907 Hague Convention was included in this decree law that Bosnia-Herzegovina acceded to in terms of ratification of treaties, and if I am correct you answered no, it was not part of the treaties that were ratified or acceded to by this decree law. Is that correct, Mr. Brkic?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that I've been able to go through the list quickly, this list containing 30 different conventions, I simply didn't observe this particular convention on the list, or as being included in the decree law. It may be an erroneous conclusion. All I'm saying is that I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Brkic, it's been brought out on cross-examination that you have experience not only as a military attorney and certainly in drafting many of the laws that we've reviewed, and also someone who teaches humanitarian law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the 1907 Hague Convention that regulates the war of armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, if possible, what its status is under international law?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That sounds like the sort of legal question which the witness said he wouldn't answer and he's not here as an expert on those matters. It's a matter for Your Honours, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Objection sustained. If you want to make a submission on the current status under international law of that convention you're free to do, so but the witness is here not as a legal expert, but I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, yes. Then I'll withdraw that question and ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, when Bosnia was ratifying various international conventions on law of war, do you know whether it was necessary for Bosnia to ratify the 1907 Hague Convention in order to be bound by it?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the beginning of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It would have been necessary for that convention to be ratified too by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I explained that due to the fact that there were no copies of these conventions to be had, and that was the reason why most of the conventions were not adopted or ratified by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would it be your testimony that after this decree law was published in the gazette on the 15th November 1992, or before that, that Bosnia as an independent country was not bound by the 1907 Hague Convention?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we first ascertain that on the 6th of April 1992, or rather on the 1st of March, Bosnia and Herzegovina acquired independence, that it had not previously as an independent state ratified any of the conventions, the answer that follows is no. However, as up until that date, Bosnia and Herzegovina had been part of the former Yugoslavia, which had been ratifying all the conventions successively from a wide range of different areas, then it would have been quite logical to expect. It's just that I can't confirm now whether the decree law on the adoption of regulations and provisions from the former Yugoslavia, whether that indeed comprised the conventions or not. But it only would have been to be expected that this continuity issue should exist and that the transition from the former Yugoslavia to all the new states that were created in the area should be a logical one. As I said yesterday, the Criminal Code of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted by Bosnia-Herzegovina as its own. And Article 16 comprises virtually all of the international crimes against the international -- against international law which also includes most of the war crimes. And it would follow that on the 2nd, 3rd or 5th of April whenever Official Gazette number 2 was published, Bosnia-Herzegovina indirectly, perhaps at a stretch, adopted these conventions as its own and what follows is that these crimes against international law were, in fact, embodied in the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, Madam Sellers, please. Was succession under international law specifically dealt with when the new state of Bosnia and Herzegovina came into existence, or was it left completely out to apply under the strict rule of international law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, for a state to be internationally recognised, it must have its own unique legal system and the armed forces to protect it. At the moment of its recognition, Bosnia-Herzegovina had no legal system in place, nor did it have any armed forces, nor had it been recognised by the United Nations. In order to build a legal system of its own, in a way, since it was own a republic with specific laws governing the republican provisions, at the very outset Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted this decree law prescribing the specific areas of life of the economy, of defence, of mining, if you like, would be adopting the -- all the Yugoslav provisions as their own. From that day, these provisions are considered provisions of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course you couldn't give it the name of the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina because that sort of thing had already existed and these provisions regulate the general area of law and also the specific parts that were not regulated by the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Likewise, the same law on the same day prescribed which laws would not be applied as Bosnia-Herzegovina's. So that in a certain way, by adopting the regulations in a formal and legal sense, by a legislative body, a certain legal system was inaugurated. In parallel to setting up of the staff of the Territorial Defence, in a bid to establish an armed force they would protect this legal system, thereby bestowing on Bosnia-Herzegovina the status of an internationally recognised state. Or at least that is my understanding of the matter. So the answer is, it wasn't an automatic thing. It was adopted at the time, but there was a succession of other laws and regulations that were adopted over time to be superseded by new domestic provisions at some point in the future, as was the case with the provisions governing the work of the armed forces.
