utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you also testified on redirect that in order to be a recognised member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that one had to have insignias on their clothes if they didn't have uniforms. Now, in terms of insignias, would an insignia just have to be some type of identifying element so that units could recognise each other and be distinguished from the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, it needs to be an open question or would it have to be the official lily emblem, since that is what we were asking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, that does not have to be the question, Your Honour, excuse me. I believe that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question, Mr. Jones, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, if you could answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you could repeat your question, Ms. Sellers, or I can read it out for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The question is in the transcript, Mr. Brkic, you testified on redirect that in order to be a recognised member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that one had to have insignia on their clothes if they didn't have uniforms. Now, in terms of insignia, would an insignia have to be some type of identifying element so the units could recognise each other and be distinguished from the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that according to the standards envisaged by the Geneva Conventions, for someone to be considered a warring party, they must meet all these conditions to have an organisational structure, to be led by a commander and to have insignia. These were cumulative conditions that needed to be met in order to be considered a warring party and as such, subject to international conventions. An absence of insignia might be just a matter of a given point in time, what marks of distinction certain people decided to use. But there needed to be an existing provision in order to satisfy these cumulative criteria, to be considered as a warring party. And that's why the presidency tasked someone to have this provision written so that once an armed force was set up, all the troops had the same uniform, the same system of ranks, and the same insignia that would distinguish them as members of a certain army. I can't say for sure but I know that at the outset, there were 6.000 plastic badges with the coat of arms that were produced in Sarajevo. I'm not sure if they were delivered to other areas too, and I can't say which insignia were worn by any other units. This is really not something that in all honesty I can testify about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brkic. And then final question in this area, Mr. Brkic. You've mentioned that there were certain criteria, five criteria, in addition to insignia. Would you just tell the Trial Chamber -- would you clarify your evidence there? What other criteria would you look for to see if someone would come under -- I believe your testimony was under the law of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who would have been considered a warring party and subject to international conventions, this body should have an organisational structure, it should be armed, it should be led by a commander, and it should have marks of distinction or insignia, distinguishing features.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could distinguishing features be armbands or ribbons or different colour top? Would that be distinguishing features?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. You needed to be able to draw a distinction based on something. Now, whether this could be considered a legal feature and to be included in the definition of those cumulative criteria, I'm not sure about that, but you needed to be able to tell the warring parties apart. At one point certainly there would be a great deal of confusion on the ground, and insignia would cease to matter, and therefore a commander would order for purposes of identification that his own units wear insignia that were different from some of his other units and particularly from the enemy, especially in cases where the enemy happened to be wearing similar clothes or insignia. When I was a member of the infantry in the JNA, we wore different kinds of insignia and we played out a conflict scenario.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask a couple of questions about an area that was covered in redirect, and it concerned the former JNA regulations and then the rules on service that you drafted or supervised. You testified that originally in the JNA regulations there were about 694 articles, but in the new rules on service, the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they only had about 81 items. Now, among those 81 items, there are items that talk about respect for international law and other issues. Now, the respect for international law, was that something that is a new article that only came about with your drafting of the rules on service, or is that an article that carried over from the JNA regulations?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer -- I can't answer the latter part of the question for the simple reason that I don't remember. The former part of the question I can answer in this way. We wanted to make the life of soldiers and military units completely organised from the time they got up in the morning until the time they went to sleep, including the guards' night shift or various peculiar situations when someone was killed when there was a funeral to be attended, that sort of thing. I assume - and that's as much as I can do at this point in time - that the same principle was enshrined in the old rules, in the old manual for the JNA, but that's just an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would that principle from your drafting of the new rules, that principle that relates to international law and international military law, was that important enough to carry over into the rules of service of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was very important in my opinion for the simple reason that within a 24-hour period, because that's how long a day lasts, you could have a combat situation. In addition to sleeping, in addition to training, there could be combat situation occurring, regardless of the time of day. Any member of the armed forces when facing a combat situation is responsible in a particular way to apply the order issued on the 20th of June, or rather the 23rd of August, the order to apply the international rules of war. We hereby wished also to have covered this particular section of internal life, if you like, the internal life of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now on redirect, you were asked to remember the statement that was taken by the Office of the Prosecutor, and in particular, that section of the statement that spoke of the JNA regulations on service and then the subsequent rules on service in the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I go back to that same part of the statement because it appears in the statement, and I quote, that in relationship to the rules and the service in the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that you edited after consultation with Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina TO or Territorial Defence. Now, you consulted with the Territorial Defence, and could you tell the Trial Chamber in your consultation with the Territorial Defence, did they approve of the inclusion of all of those 81 articles?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, could you just tell us at what time period, if you remember, what month did you hold the consultation with Territorial Defence of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in regard to these rules on service?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I emphasised several times that all the drafts were made at the same time, and this includes the rules governing the work of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These provisions were then delivered to the defence ministry and the justice ministry, and they all made certain remarks. I can't give you a set date, but I can say that consultations were done before the date that was set as the date of the adoption of the relevant law. So if we are talking about the 1st of August, all consultations plus the final draft must have been delivered to a legislative body for approval as a law of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina just before. The consultations among the various ministries, the defence ministry, the Main Staff of the TO, the justice ministry, the ministry of health and all the other ministries each for their own area, so these consultations might have taken between seven and 10 days at the very most.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would those consultations have taken place in the month of May 1992 or June 1992 or July 1992 or August 1992? If you could just clarify a bit for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that it could have been August or July rather than May, because it was back in May that we sort of started out drafting these provisions and regulations. I don't believe that it was done at that time. The process of drafting these laws climaxed in a manner of speaking in July, rather late June and early July. July was a critical month to round the whole thing off, the whole legislation, as it related to the armed forces. I can't say for sure -- I can't even give you a ballpark figure when exactly all these provisions were adopted. I know it was summer. It was a hot day. I brought the rules back to my clerk to have them revised, for errors. It might have been late July or mid-August. No, not even mid-August. It must have been late July. It was still summertime.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers. There are no questions from the Bench, Professor Brkic, which means that we have come to the end of your testimony. You are free to go. You will very soon be escorted out of the courtroom by Madam Usher and you will receive, of course, all the assistance you require by our staff to facilitate your return back home at the earliest opportunity. On behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, who couldn't be with us these two days, and of course on my own behalf I wish to thank you for having accepted to come forward -- come here and give evidence as a witness for the Prosecution, and on behalf of everyone present here, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Likewise, I wish to thank the Trial Chamber. I wish to thank both the OTP and the Defence as well as the accused. I wish to thank you for giving me this honour, 13 or 14 years later, to remember exactly what it was that I did at the time. To remember the effort that I made to contribute to some extent to establishing some sort of legal system and continuity in Bosnia-Herzegovina the way it was at the time. So once again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll reconvene on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will reconvene on Monday, all right? Next week we'll issue a scheduling order indicating when you are expected to rest your case. That will be the 1st of June, right? And allocating the 2nd of June for submissions by the Defence and the 3rd of June by submissions from the Prosecution for the purpose of the Rule 98 bis exercise which is our responsibility. I thank you. I will see you again on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, 23 May 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.46 a.m.,
